item.title: Sqwod Daily — Thursday, 23 July 2026
item.description: When a hardware giant buys the software your clients plan their lives around, 'platform risk' stops being a buzzword.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday, 23 July 2026 View online →
DAILY
The fitness industry, decoded — in five minutes.
Thursday, 23 July 2026 · Weekday
When a hardware giant buys the software your clients plan their lives around, 'platform risk' stops being a buzzword.
— Sqwod
Money movement
⇄  Acquired
Garmin / TrainingPeaks
 —
Garmin acquires TrainingPeaks, raising questions about platform pricing, integrations, and data ownership for coaches
Connect the dots
Garmin + TrainingPeaks: who really owns your programming?
TrainingPeaks has long been the invisible backbone of serious training — coaches build plans there, athletes live there, and everyone quietly assumed it would stay neutral. Garmin just ended that assumption. An acquisition folds a software platform into a hardware ecosystem, and the history of those mergers is pretty consistent: integrations tighten, pricing evolves, and the new parent's devices get the best data treatment first.
For studio operators and coaches, the concrete risk is dependency. If your entire client programming stack lives in one platform that now answers to a device manufacturer, your leverage just shrank. This week's action is simple: audit where your programming actually lives. Do you have exportable copies? Are your athletes locked to a Garmin-native experience to get full value? Diversification isn't paranoia — it's ops hygiene.
The rundown
01
$200 Screenless: Garmin Takes a Shot at Whoop's Wrist
Garmin just dropped a $200 screen-free fitness band aimed squarely at Whoop's territory. For coaches and studio operators who recommend wearables to clients, there's a new name in the no-display game worth knowing.
Source: Athletech News →
02
DSSV drops 2026 DACH fitness industry benchmarks
The DSSV has unveiled the key figures shaping the German-speaking fitness market in 2026. If you run a gym or coach clients in the region, this is the data that tells you where the money and membership trends are actually heading.
Source: DSSV →
03
body LIFE is gating a live studio-ops webinar behind a password
The protected session promises top-tier expertise delivered directly to studio owners and coaches — if you're in the industry, hunting down that access code is worth five minutes of your morning.
Source: body LIFE →
04
Movement is Therapy — and Wolfgang Unsöld Has the Receipts
Trainingsworld spotlights Wolfgang Unsöld's case for movement as a therapeutic tool — a timely reminder that what you're selling in your studio isn't just fitness, it's function and wellbeing.
Source: Trainingsworld →
05
Garmin Just Bought TrainingPeaks — Here's What Changes for You
Garmin has acquired TrainingPeaks, and if your clients live and die by their training plans, this merger is worth watching. Platform integrations, pricing, and data ownership could all shift — so now's a good time to know where your programming lives.
Source: Lifehacker →
06
New London gym puts recovery and wellness front and centre
London Post spotlights a brand-new gym built around injury recovery and wellness — a reminder for operators that the 'fix you up' niche is quietly becoming the whole pitch.
Source: London Post →
Stat
$200
Price of Garmin's new screen-free fitness band
It's the clearest signal yet that the no-display wearable category is becoming competitive — coaches who recommend hardware to clients now have a second credible option, and Whoop has a price-point fight on its hands.
Sqwod recs
✓ Steal: Reframe one service tier on your website around function and recovery outcomes rather than sweat metrics — 'move better, hurt less' converts differently than 'burn more.' Test it on a single class or programme description first.
✓ Try: Run a 10-minute 'movement screen' as your standard new-client intake instead of a fitness assessment — it positions you as a movement professional from session one and opens natural upsell conversations around corrective work and longevity.

item.content:encoded:
Wednesday, 22 July 2026 View online →
DAILY
The fitness industry, decoded — in five minutes.
Wednesday, 22 July 2026 · Weekday
The biggest tie-up in fitness tech this year wants to 'prescribe' your workout — literally.
— Sqwod
Money movement
⇄  Acquired
EGYM & Playlist
 $7.5B
a reported tie-up that could turn structured training into prescribed, outcome-based fitness
Connect the dots
Fitness is being rebuilt as prescribed, outcome-based medicine
A reported $7.5B tie-up between EGYM and Playlist could turn structured, data-driven training into something closer to a prescription — the right dose of the right movement for the right person. Meanwhile Planet Fitness admitted its strength pivot went too far, and Hyrox keeps globalizing competitive fitness. The market is splitting into prescribed outcomes on one end and mass participation on the other.
For operators, the EGYM–Playlist signal is the one to internalize: 'give everyone the same class' is losing to 'give this person their dose.' Personalized, measurable programming is becoming the product — and that's a game a good coach can play better than an app.
The rundown
01
EGYM and Playlist's reported $7.5B tie-up could 'prescribe' fitness
The vision: structured training that works like a prescription — the right dose for the right person. Prescribed, measurable programming is becoming the product.
Source: Athletech News →
02
Planet Fitness admits its strength pivot went too far
A rare public walk-back. The lesson: read your own members before chasing a trend — overshooting a pivot costs more than moving deliberately.
Source: Athletech News →
03
Hyrox expands its global race calendar with multi-week events
Competitive fitness as mass participation keeps scaling worldwide. If your members love a challenge, Hyrox-style events are a proven engagement and revenue engine.
Source: Athletech News →
04
Les Mills launches its first-ever reformer Pilates program
The group-fitness giant is entering reformer Pilates. When Les Mills moves, thousands of studios follow — expect reformer programming to spread fast.
Source: Athletech News →
05
EoS Fitness opens 9 gyms in a single quarter
A blistering Texas-led expansion pace. Proof the value-gym model still has aggressive runway when the operations are dialed in.
Source: Athletech News →
06
Garmin debuts a $200 screenless band aimed at Whoop
A screenless tracker at $200, from a GPS-and-sensor heavyweight, lands right in Whoop's lane. The client conversation about subscription-free tracking just got easier.
Source: Athletech News →

A deal this size around prescribed, data-driven training tells you where the industry's smart money sees the future: outcomes, not access.

Franchising is quietly betting big on two words: longevity and 'soft.'
— Sqwod
Money movement

Connect the dots
The next franchise gold rush is longevity, not HIIT
An Ultimate Longevity Center concept sold 200 franchise territories before it even fully launched, while the industry is naming a 'soft fitness' era — recovery, mobility, and low-intensity training moving to the center. The high-burn, high-churn model is losing ground to formats people can sustain and franchisees can bank on.
For operators, this is the clearest demand signal of the summer: build for longevity and recovery, not just intensity. The consumer wants to feel better for longer — and investors are funding exactly that.

The low-cost model still has runway in under-served geographies. A reminder that 'the market is saturated' is usually only true for one format at a time.

The 'soft fitness' era is officially here
Recovery, mobility, and low-intensity training are moving to the center of the offer. The stuff that used to be the cool-down is becoming the main event.

item.title: Sqwod Daily — Friday, 17 July 2026
item.description: Consolidation on one side, consumer protection on the other — the rules of the gym business are being rewritten this week.
item.content:encoded:
Friday, 17 July 2026 View online →
DAILY
The fitness industry, decoded — in five minutes.
Friday, 17 July 2026 · Weekday
Consolidation on one side, consumer protection on the other — the rules of the gym business are being rewritten this week.
— Sqwod
Money movement
⇄  Acquired
Interactive Strength
 —
acquires connected stair-climbing brand Stepr
Connect the dots
The gym business is getting both bigger and better-behaved
Interactive Strength is acquiring connected stair-climber brand Stepr, rolling up hardware under one roof, while New York became the first US city to force click-to-cancel on gym memberships. Growth by acquisition on one hand; a crackdown on the industry's oldest retention trick on the other.
The operators who thrive won't be the ones clinging to hard-to-cancel contracts — those days are ending. They'll be the ones so good at delivering value that nobody wants to cancel in the first place. Make leaving easy and staying worth it.
The rundown
01
Interactive Strength acquires connected stair-climber Stepr
Rolling specialized hardware under one roof, the deal signals the connected-fitness shakeout is entering its buy-or-be-bought phase. Watch who's next.
Source: Athletech News →
02
NYC becomes first US city to force click-to-cancel on gyms
The industry's oldest retention trick is on borrowed time. The winning move: make leaving easy and staying worth it, before regulation makes the choice for you.
Source: Athletech News →
03
Investors tip Pilates and low-price gyms for growth
Where the smart money sees the next few years. A useful map to check your own expansion or format bets against before you commit capital.
Source: Athletech News →
04
Echelon makes its case for connected strength
The connected-fitness brand is betting the next home category is strength, not cardio. Worth knowing where the equipment giants think the puck is going.
Source: Athletech News →
05
ATN Insights: driving revenue with movement assessments
A good assessment is better coaching and a natural upsell in one. If you're not screening new clients, you're leaving both results and revenue on the table.
Source: Athletech News →
Policy watch
NYC adopts click-to-cancel for gym memberships
New York is the first US city to require easy online cancellation for gyms — a signal that hard-to-quit contracts are on borrowed time everywhere. Get ahead of it: make leaving simple before you're forced to.
Sqwod recs
✓ Steal: Turn your cancellation page into a save-and-goodwill moment: offer a pause option and a genuine 'no hard feelings' — members who leave clean come back and refer far more than trapped ones.
✓ Read: Investors tipping Pilates and low-price gyms for growth is a useful map of where the smart money sees the next few years — worth a scan before your next big bet.

item.content:encoded:

DAILY
The fitness industry, decoded — in five minutes.
Tuesday, 14 July 2026 · Weekday
When a supplement brand raises a billion and hires like Nike, 'wellness startup' stops being a cute label.
— Sqwod
Money movement
▲  Raise
IM8 (Prenetics)
 $1B
David Beckham's supplement brand takes growth capital from General Catalyst's CVF
Connect the dots
The wellness brands are now operating like consumer giants
David Beckham's IM8 pulled in $1B of growth capital from General Catalyst, and Whoop hired a former Nike marketing chief to run its brand. Different companies, same signal: the category's leaders are capitalizing and staffing like mass-market consumer businesses, not scrappy health startups.
For a coach or operator, that's the competitive context for everything you do. The brands your clients follow now have Nike-tier marketing and nine-figure war chests — so your edge isn't budget, it's the trust and the in-person relationship they can't buy.
The rundown
01
Beckham's IM8 secures $1B from General Catalyst
The supplement brand, owned by Prenetics, took a billion in growth capital via General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund. Wellness brands are now scaling like consumer giants.
Source: Athletech News →
02
Whoop names former Nike exec Dirk-Jan van Hameren as CMO
A recovery-tracker company hiring Nike-tier marketing talent tells you the next wearables battle is brand, not sensors. Storytelling is the new spec sheet.
Source: Storyboard18 →

Monday's theme: the tech is finally catching up to the athlete — for better and for worse.
— Sqwod
Connect the dots
More data isn't the same as better coaching
Swimmers are getting purpose-built underwater audio, brands are being told to prep for an 'autonomous age' of AI, and yet the industry is quietly admitting a hard truth: piling on wearable data hasn't automatically made anyone healthier or better-coached.
That gap — between data collected and behavior changed — is the whole opportunity for a human coach. The tech captures the numbers; you're the one who turns them into a decision the client actually acts on.

item.description: Two demographics are quietly reshaping the floor plan: kids, and people who want to train for decades.
item.content:encoded:
Friday, 10 July 2026 View online →
DAILY
The fitness industry, decoded — in five minutes.
Friday, 10 July 2026 · Weekday
Two demographics are quietly reshaping the floor plan: kids, and people who want to train for decades.
— Sqwod
Connect the dots
The market is aging up and down at the same time
Youth fitness is booming while adult members increasingly say they want 'sustainable' workouts they can do for life. Both trends point away from the burn-it-down, beach-body model and toward longevity — training as maintenance, not punishment.
That's a programming and messaging shift, not just a vibe. The operators who win the next five years will be the ones selling 'still moving at 80,' not 'shredded by summer.'
The rundown
01
Youth fitness is booming, despite the challenges
New data shows kids and teens entering structured fitness in bigger numbers. For operators, that's a real revenue line and a family-membership hook, not an afterthought.

Members want 'sustainable' workouts, report finds
Adults increasingly want training they can keep doing for decades, not a six-week crash. The shift from shred-for-summer to longevity is a messaging opportunity.

Kineon's Move+ stands out with a laser + red-light combo
A recovery device pairing two light therapies in one unit. Recovery tech keeps getting more accessible — worth knowing when clients ask what actually works.

— Sqwod
Money movement

 $61M
acquires German brand wellyou to deepen its DACH footprint
Connect the dots
Consolidation and DTC are happening at once — and DACH is the prize
Basic-Fit just spent $61M to fold German brand wellyou into its empire, while TRX went the other way and launched its own retail line. One is buying market share, the other is building it — but both are chasing the same thing: a direct line to the member.
For operators in German-speaking markets, the Basic-Fit move is the one to sit with. When Europe's biggest low-cost chain pays up specifically to deepen its DACH footprint, it's telling you exactly where it thinks the growth is — and it might be your postcode.

Europe's biggest low-cost chain is paying up to deepen its DACH footprint. For German-speaking operators, that's a giant getting bigger in your backyard — plan accordingly.
